Is this a decent acoustic guitar to start with?

I'm not looking to perform or anything. I simply want to sit around my house and play with songs I like. Best I can tell, the only thing I'd be missing with this package is a capo. I don't care to have a slide.

The short answer: yes, that looks like a decent guitar, and with a very complete set of goodies.

The long answer: you should really go to a music store and try out different guitars. Maybe take someone with you who knows something about guitars and plays themselves. Different guitars, even within the same brand, can have quite a different feel and sound, and that is not something you can judge over the internet. Furthermore, it's great fun to try out guitars for an afternoon and go home with what feels best. Maybe you won't get all the goodies for the same money, but you sure will get the best guitar your budget can buy.

And a tip for the bar chords: move your thumb down the neck, a little bit towards the body, so that the pressure comes from the torsion of your wrist, and not the strength of your index finger.

The nearest guitar store is quite a bit away, unfortunately, but the way you explained the trip makes me wanna rethink the distance being an issue.

And wow...I've mentioned the bar chord thing to a few people before and no one has ever explained it like you did. While I'm sure the discomfort won't go away completely right off the bat, I imagine I'll be able to get used to it before too long.

Thank you so much for your insight. I can't wait to try these things!

No worries, glad to help. You could also get a good second-hand one from closer to you, I'm sure.

Anyway, you'll find that some guitars let you play bar chords easier than others - i.e. require less pressure. That has to do with the distance of the strings to the neck. Generally, the closer the strings are to the neck, the easier to play a bar chord - but if the strings are too close, they hit the neck when you play them and you get buzz.Also, you can buy thinner strings that are easier to play, but detune faster than thicker strings. One more thing: if you go to the store, buy the guitar you tested, not 'the same one' from a box, they're different.
Put in the work and the instrument matters less. If you enjoy it then it will be great.

Is the action the thing that holds up the strings? So that means not having to push down as hard? I imagine the trade-off, then, is that it's easier to accidentally push it into contact with the frets...not like that's a huge deal, now that I think about it.

So if that is the action, what's the advantage/disadvantage of a high vs. low action? (I realize I could Google this, and I'm happy to if you don't wanna type it out, but I prefer conversation.)

Action is the distance between the strings and the fretboard. Typically yahamas are not TOO low and you rarely hit other strings by accident. Guitars with high action will make you NOT want to play guitar. I typically teach kids so this is HUGE for their tiny hands. Even if you don't do barre chords, and you have high action even with light gauge strings (thin ones), the strings will feel they are cutting into your fingers. The reason electric guitars are easy to play is because the action is super low and gauge of the strings is thin. Acoustic dreadnought bodies require typically medium gauge and is what you're looking into. You might want to look into an auditorium style body. They use lighter gauge by default and CAN be easier.
